sections.overview: The European plaice is a right-eyed flatfish of the continental shelf of north-western Europe, found from Iceland and the White Sea southward along the European coast. It is one of the best-studied fish of the North Sea and has been fished there for centuries.
sections.identification: The upper side is brown or greenish-brown with irregular bright red or orange spots, and the underside is white. The skin is smooth with small scales, and a bony ridge runs behind the eyes. Common length is about 40 cm, and the largest fish reach about 100 cm and 7 kg.
sections.habitat: It lives on sandy and muddy bottoms from the shore down to about 200 m, usually at 10–50 m, in water of 2–15 °C. Juveniles stay in shallow coastal water and outer estuaries and move deeper as they grow; in the North Sea the Wadden Sea is the most important nursery.
sections.diet: Adults feed mainly on thin-shelled molluscs and polychaete worms, taking bivalves, the siphons of buried clams and, locally, small crustaceans and brittle stars. Adults do not feed during the spawning period.
sections.behavior: It rests on the seabed partly buried in sediment. Tagging showed that individuals return to the same spawning and feeding areas, and adults travel between them by using tidal streams: they drift in midwater with the current and stay on the bottom when it turns.
sections.reproduction: Spawning takes place offshore in restricted areas, peaking in early January in the eastern Channel and mid-February in the German Bight. A 35 cm female may produce 60,000–100,000 pelagic eggs of 1.7–2.2 mm. The eggs and larvae drift for three to four months; the fish settles on the bottom only after metamorphosis, when the left eye has moved to the right side. In the North Sea, males mature at two to three years and females at four to five.
sections.ecology: Plaice larvae eat small planktonic animals such as appendicularians and copepods, while older fish feed on the seabed. The eggs are eaten by other fish: many were found in herring and sprat stomachs, so egg survival varies with their abundance.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern (assessed 2022, as reported by FishBase). It is an important commercial species, taken mostly by beam trawls in a mixed fishery with sole. In the North Sea, landings rose from about 70,000 t in the late 1950s to about 170,000 t in the late 1980s, then fell below 60,000 t by 2005, and earlier maturation has been linked to fishing pressure.
